Juveniles of the sand sea star Astropecten irregularis undergo a critical developmental milestone during larval metamorphosis, a period of profound body plan reorganisation. The recently metamorphosed juvenile possesses an arm length of just 0.5 cm , a size that marks the transition from a planktonic to a benthic existence. This initial arm length is measured at a stable water temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], a thermal regime typical of its shallow, sandy-bottom habitats in the northeastern Atlantic. The mass of an individual at this early stage, effectively its wet weight at birth, is remarkably low at 0.0000042 grams [Wwb = 0.0000042 grams], reflecting the diminutive size of the fertilized ovum from which it develops. This minuscule initial mass, derived from an egg with a diameter of about 200 micrometers, represents the entire material endowment inherited from the maternal parent. The energy reserves packed into this small volume must sustain the larva through its planktotrophic feeding phase and the energetically costly process of metamorphosis, after which the juvenile begins its life on the seafloor.

As the post-metamorphic juvenile grows, it progresses through a series of allometric shifts leading to sexual maturation. The onset of puberty, defined by the first detectable signs of gonad maturation, is correlated with the animal reaching a specific body size rather than a fixed age under the local thermal conditions. Field surveys indicate that individuals attain an arm length of 2.4 cm [Lp = 2.4 cm] at this critical juncture, a size that signals the allocation of resources toward reproductive development. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is estimated at 4.7 grams [Wwp = 4.7 grams], a value derived from the cubed relationship between length and mass relative to the ultimate adult dimensions. This weight represents a substantial investment in somatic tissue before the individual begins diverting energy toward gamete production. The timing of this event is also notable, occurring approximately 912.5 days after birth [tp = approximately 912.5 days after birth] when maintained at 14 °C [T = 14 °C], a duration that reflects the relatively slow pace of life in a temperate-water echinoderm.

At the peak of the reproductively active adult phase, the gonadosomatic index (GSI) was determined. For A. irregularis, this index reached 42% [GSI = 42%] when measured at 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. This measurement was obtained from specimens collected during the peak of the breeding season in the North Sea.

The ultimate arm length, representing the maximum size achievable by a fully grown adult, provides a clear upper boundary for the species' growth trajectory. Long-term population studies have established that the sand sea star has a fully grown adult arm length of 6.6 cm [Li = 6.6 cm], a modest dimension compared to some of its larger congeneric relatives such as Astropecten aranciacus. From this linear measure, the corresponding ultimate wet weight is calculated to be 97 grams [Wwi = 97 grams], based on the total arm plus disk length of a typical large specimen measuring 124.55 mm. This asymptotic body mass represents the culmination of a long period of somatic growth, after which reproductive output becomes the primary physiological focus. The maximum lifespan of an individual under these thermal conditions is approximately 1,825 days [am = approximately 1,825 days] at 14 °C [T = 14 °C], after which senescence and age-related mortality become increasingly likely.

The developmental timeline from birth to the onset of reproduction is tightly constrained by temperature and resource availability. Following the initial metamorphic event, the juvenile spends a relatively brief period in the most vulnerable size classes. The time since birth at metamorphosis, marking the end of the larval phase, is only 30 days after birth  when development proceeds at 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. This rapid transition from a free-swimming larva to a benthic juvenile is an adaptive strategy to minimise predation risk in the plankton, and is comparable to the brief planktonic durations observed in other temperate Astropecten species. In contrast, the journey from this post-metamorphic state to full reproductive maturity is far more protracted, taking several years, a pattern that allows the individual to accumulate the somatic resources necessary for the high reproductive effort that characterises the adult stage. The pace of these life-history transitions is typical for a slow-growing, iteroparous invertebrate adapted to stable temperate marine environments.
